blocks.x: The End The End Now, let's see, we'll start all over again. What's the date today, Dick, first off?
August the 3rd,
Monday, August the 3rd.
And we're here at Lano Fabos' house. Let's see, Lano Fabos, that's the only name. And what was your date of birth again?
Uh-huh. And you said that nobody in your family played music before you?
Not that I can remember.
Why did you, uh, you know, why did you want to take up music?
Well, it started on, uh, I saw a woman band at the, at the theater one day, and decided I wanted to take comfort from there. And I started taking that little man, Shawnee.
Uh-huh. Did he, uh, did he charge you for lessons, or, I mean, a regular teacher?
Oh, but I mean, a very small amount.
Oh, yeah. One of the best teachers they had to, he charged 25 cents a lesson.
Yeah.
And he wrote his own theory book for 25 cents. Gee whee. He did it for pleasure, for the New Orleans, uh, youngster to learn to play music. Uh-huh.

What did, uh, he taught you on the trumpet, huh? That's right. Did, uh, you had to take a trumpet there, or did he have a trumpet there for you? No, I had to, I had my own trumpet. Well, uh, did you start playing trumpet or cornet?
No, it, well, it was a cornet, yeah, that's right. And then you advanced on to trumpet. Uh-huh.
How long was it before you switched to trumpet? Oh, I mean, about two or three years.
Oh, no, no, no. Because I had a little cornet that's been a bag. Yeah.
But what year would that have been when you started playing around? Yeah. Hmm, very small, let me see. About, uh, about four years ago.
Yeah, four years ago. About, about thirty-six years ago. Uh-huh.
So, you'd have been what, about eighteen, twenty- I was about sixteen or seventeen. Oh, twenty-six years ago. Uh-huh. But how long did you take lessons with him?
Oh, I think, living with Shawnee, about a couple years, and then I took lessons with, uh, uh, Uh, Narmie Pond. Snire, Manny Perez, Uh-huh. and later on with, uh, several castigots.
What, um, what kind of thing did they, did they teach you? You know what I mean?
Well, they taught us regular rumors of music. I mean, uh, theory and, uh, regular progression of music.

Uh-huh. And they taught you how to read, I guess, or not? That's right, right. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Well, what do you think? What, uh, what was one of the first bands? Can you remember any of the first bands you played with? You know, first band?
First band, uh, well, I don't know, well, the, uh, Starlight Serenade. Uh-huh. Who was in that band?
Uh, Wilton Smith.

Wilton Smith. Yeah, Wilton Smith. Uh, Wilton Smith, uh, What dance band did he play? Saxophone. And, uh, little Pappy played drums. Yeah, Wilton Smith played drums. Ratliff. And, uh, what was Pappy's writing then? Uh, Clarence Ratliff. And, uh, Sue Ross was in that band. Peter Pass was in that band. And, uh, and, uh, In relation to honor?
It had two trumpets in their band. And who was in that band? Clarence Ratliff.
And who was in that band? Peter Pass was in that band.
And it all had two trumpets in that band.
Two trumpets.
In relation to Honor of the Pass?
I can't quite remember who was in that band. What kind of band was it? It was a little five or six piece of music. Did you play for music? I used to play off little choruses written down.
What kind of places did that band play?
I played house parties.
Did you get paid for playing?
Oh sure, we got paid.
So in other words when you first started playing you started earning money.
Well the money was small but it usually didn't.
How long did you stay with that bunch? Oh I guess we had been about a year or two.
I know.
Well what did you leave them or you went better off them?
Oh well you know you go with different outfits. Each one will try to get better outfits. Yeah yeah.
What did you go with after that? I think Moonlight Center was the one that we put after that.
Was that George Augustine? No that was Sidney Cage in that bunch. I don't know.
Remember who else was in that band?
Oh I really knew she was on the way back there. That one Sidney Cage was on that bunch with anything?
Well the first Moonlight Center was Henry Cosnar, you know what I mean? That was you? That was you? Yeah. And after that there's a band then he'd take me there.

Yeah. He kept the Navi Moonlight Center. And then all night they'd been over again. Yeah. And then Tibor Briscoe playing saxophone. Old man Bill, he's working at Crouse playing bass. And Neumon Reese playing drum. He's with Brunus' band now. Oh yeah. And Aston Murray playing piano. No it wasn't Aston Murray, was it Regal Boy playing piano then? And Will White playing trumpet. And Nase Fountain playing trombone. I think.
Two trumpets he had there? Yeah, two trumpets.
Yeah, it had to be a band. Lee Woozong playing tennis sax. I don't know if Oscar was playing with the outfit or not, then Oscar was on.
What kind of band was that? I mean there were straight arrangements in this band?
Well they were pretty fair. It was a nice band. Mostly orchestration.
Yeah, mostly orchestration, that's right. Did you ever in those early days play much head stuff? Well now and then you've really just played it.
I mean not the band. Yeah well of course, yeah. Yeah.
Line over the floor from the beginning. If somebody asked for a number, he would write it. Yeah. Whether he know how to play it or not, he'd write it and put it in front of him.
Uh huh. In other words, he always was a first trumpet man.

Yeah, first trumpet man. First trumpet man. He would write it. So the head numbers, he can play all these head numbers. But if a line doesn't come on the job, a line doesn't have a stack of paper like that. When you call the number, he'll put it in front of him.
He's still there.
Yeah.
Yeah. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

Mm-hm. You know it might seem odd, but at that time, for like, what's his name? Cuckoo. Cuckoo. You know I used to like to hear Cuckoo play. And then now the Cuckoo is- Well Cuckoo was a pretty good trumpet. Yeah, he was a pretty good trumpet at that time. And what was his set up for there? Louis Dumaine. And the set up when he used to work at the Broom place there. Maurice Duran. Maurice Duran. Yeah, I was proud of him.
He used to play in the alley right by the Seminole Market on the side that was the alley. And quite nice to know. The cab right there, he called it the alley.

And on the dry too? He was a top man. It was nice to sit in the shore, he used to play the lyrics, sit in the shore and then listen down and play. And it was Mayor Perez, he was the first one to start that wild wild music. I mean, and Buzz had picked it up after that, but he was the one who would really make it.

In other words, I mean, which is, honestly, what do you mean like street advertisements and we used to hear that at that time, you know, that maybe you want to ask them on that. Did you ever work on the street at that time? No, in the bands.
What band you like on the advertisements? You know, I used to play the advertisements like, you know, Gilbert Renier, Chris Kelly,

Punch and all that. Oh yeah, like, well, Kid Renier was another one. It was a pleasure. I mean, he was in the top lot. Oh yeah, he was a pleasure. You know, the first time I heard Kid Renier it was really odd. I had been hearing about Kid Renier for years. And when I heard him and I saw him, in fact, he didn't even seem to be a type of man to me. I thought he was a great big fella, the way he used to talk about him, but he was a very small fella. Yes, he got him to take. And when I heard him play, so I asked a lot of fun, I said, well, I said, that man's a real Trump player, who is he? He said, you don't know that, that's Kid Renier. Yeah, he really was a fine Trump player. You remember him?
I met him one time.
Oh yeah, I mean, did you hear him when he was in his head there?
No, but he came back on two numbers and really cut those.
Oh, he was a fine Trump player.

I couldn't believe it. All of a sudden, he just took five. When we were playing at the Gypsy Tea Room, Don Redmond come down with that big, beautiful, fine band out of New York, and he had a lovely big band, a 16 piece band, and we had I think six pieces. And Don Redmond said, hi in the world, can that trumpet player play all night like that, and it don't ever look like he get tired. Every number Kid Renier played was just like, the last number was like the first number.

Yeah, he was a good trumpet player. See, the fellas, what he was talking, first, I mean, there's first class musicians. I just broke it down. You know, the ordinary fellas, like what I'm talking about, Chris Kelly time. I don't remember Chris Kelly really.
Well I mean the fellas we had first started to talk about. Now I didn't know him personally, but I heard Buddy Petit several times on these parades, you know, but I didn't know him personally.

In fact I was a little small boy at that time. I mean you say that you like René and people like that, and Kukku. But was your style of trumpet playing, did it sound anything like those guys at all, or was it a totally different sound?

Well I tell you, René was a clean-cut trumpet player. He played a lot, he played a lot, he played a lot, he played quite a bit. But he had a pretty nice, clean way of playing, and I would like, if I could have played like that.
But you weren't playing too much like that, I mean you didn't sort of sound like that.

Well I wouldn't really know, because I mean it's been years, you know, and you'd have to listen to the style, because even from the time I started, from the way I play now, I mean I've changed quite a bit.

Line of it is more the style of Manuel Perez and I know him at Twy, you know them great trumpets. It's more of the musical ability. Yeah, you know, it's more in that order, you see. Everything got to be done right.
You know what he be doing.

You see them fellas when they couldn't play a piece, or remember a piece, they had a good air and they make a run or something, you know, fill it in. But trumpet players like Lionel, or I'd say my friend Leo, or Manuel Perez, or Norma Twy, or Maurice Duran, or Willie Paggio. Well that's a class of Lionel.

I'll tell you another good trumpet player, he played Dixieland too. He used to play with, I can't think of that man's name right now, he used to play with Pichon, when we were working with Pichon. From here? Yeah, he lived uptown. He and Louis, to me, he's a very good friend. He's got with Gaudet. Gaudet, that's right.
We had a boy here playing just like Gaudet, just coming, well anyhow him, he'd been sick in the hospital and he's out now, Joe Bentley.
Oh Gaudet, yeah.
He played a couple of parades, I mean he played just like Gaudet. Of course Gaudet was a little more powerful than him, a little more solid, but he played just like Gaudet used to play.

Yeah, he played with me. Listen, I want to jump of it Dick, because you can probably fill it in later. I want to get the story on this, when we were working with Mr. Highdown out there, so I'll jump to that. Talking about when you went into the Melody Inn, you know. How did that job come about? I mean who hired you to play that job?
Well from what I can remember, I hope I have it right, the early big guard came and asked me if I wanted to work with him. So, well I had been playing with big bands before then.

Well let me tell you the story. You know more about it than me. Elec went to Peterson's music store to see about some drumsticks or something. And Peterson said, Elec, you all playing anywhere? No. They want a band down at the Melody Inn for Mr. Highdown. So, Elec said, you know, you can go and see about the job. So, Elec called me and asked me about the job. And he said, you know, you can go and see about it. So, I told him, go and see about it. So, he got lying there, I got joys getting off, and myself to go around there.
So, in other words, it was a big odd job.
Yeah, at the first, when Heidel had it, it was a big odd job.
Yeah, I see. What, you remember when you first opened up that place? You remember the first night or anything about that?

Well, I'll tell you one thing, it sounded like a joke, but from the first night we started, everything went right along. Mr. Highdown was well satisfied, and the crowd, they used to, I mean, they had pretty nice attention.
He was on the floor, they had a long corner about 15 weeks.
The first we played on the floor when we first started playing.

It was mostly a lunch place and he decided to get music. He was on the floor. And then the second week he put a little rope around us to give people, and the third week he talked about it, he said, I think I'm going to get rid of this corner, lunch corner. And then he got a band stand.
Well I mean what was his business there? Was he selling drinks, night club kind of place? No.
It was thought as a sandwich and drinks, but then he discontinued the sandwich. How long did you play for?
Do you remember how long of sets used to last? Sets? Well I mean from what time did you start until you knocked off?
Oh, we worked from nine to two. That's probably.
How many nights a week would that be?
Well, first we were working three nights, Friday, Saturday, Sunday, and then he started putting Wednesday on. And then we went back to Friday, Saturday, and Sunday.
How long did you keep the band together with the same four men? Do you remember that? Oh, I see. I know it, then he said yeah.
Well we had four men together for a couple of years. Well I mean the same four. We never had four.

Or the same four. How long did George play that one? Well he had some man. Then we stayed there about two, three years after. About two years after. Yeah, and then changed from Daddy and the other. Yeah. What kind of numbers did you play? I mean what kind of numbers was the most requested of you that you can remember?

Well it was kind of hard to say exactly because we played a request program. We played pop tunes, we played Dixon and, we played rombas, tangos, all that stuff. In fact they couldn't understand how we could play such Dixon and music with four pieces like that.
They tell me that you used to pick up the piano music and write out the parts for the band. Is that right? Oh yeah, just write choruses. I know.
If nobody asked for a number like tonight, when it was our regular customers, they'd say we'll be here next weekend, or next weekend line of camera with the number row. Yeah.
That's right. Did you play every number for music or did you play? No, none of the service. Ed numbers too. None of the service.
Some of you might need to use, but some of you need to play. In fact some of you have been playing for so many years you just knew them automatically.
Did any other musicians ever come out there listening to you? Or was it just customers?
No, they used to have musicians come out there.
I mean there seemed to be a pretty famous spot where you only came out there. Very famous spot.
We used to play numbers like mumbo number five, mumbo jumbo, and things like that, and the musicians come out there and say, I feel like it isn't so good with four pieces.

Playing with receive. Listen, tell me, let me get one thing straight. What instrument did George Gano play there? He played his guitar. Electric guitar. Electric guitar. He never played a band, George? No, not there. No. Barry, I'll tell you, from the customer standpoint, I used to go out there but I gave up going
out there because I could never get close to the band. It was so packed I couldn't hear the music. Oh you went there?
I didn't know you went there. Oh yeah. Oh yeah Barry used to come there? I mean Dick. I couldn't hear the band.
It was so packed. That's the truth. You couldn't get in. Why in the world did they finally close down then?
Well what happened was that Hyde was ill and then he had a heart attack and so he sold the place to one of his employees and oddly about three weeks after he sold, he dropped
dead. He just had a heart attack? So the tiny. Yeah. The way out of it.
And then from then it went to, they kept it a while, and then who was that other fellow of that guy for?

Oh I can't think of his name but he gave Pickett a job, John Brunson, and John called me and asked him about taking the job and he would play some nights. And that's when we had went to the happy land.
One thing I wanted to ask you, when George Garner left the band, and I believe you had Smitty playing there. We had Frank Moyer first.
That fellow that was working the paddock.
Yeah Danny.

That's for him first. Well naturally he got an every night job and that's all he'd do for a living. So he took an every night job. And Lionel told me, he said, I know a good piano player. I played with him before. He named him Smitty, he said. No Wiggins played before Smitty. No Wiggins, yeah Wiggins. Not Frank Moyer. Frank Moyer, Wiggins, and then Smitty. Wiggins didn't stay, well Wiggins didn't stay long. Because he went on another job. Yeah he went on another job. And then we got Smitty. And Smitty stayed there with us all the while.
What did, let me give you one thing straight, what did you call the band? What was the name of the band?

Well at first Big Art said, told me, he said let's get some cards made, we're going to call it the Big Art Dajon Band. And then later on, he decided we're going to call it the Mighty Four. Big Art came with that name, huh? Yeah, he said we're going to call the band the Mighty Four.
The Mighty Four, that's right.
It sounded like it was a Mighty Four too, but all accounts I hear of it.
You heard it? Yeah, I heard of it. Well you heard it.

Well I mean I heard it, yeah, it would have been 15, 20 years later. No, it wouldn't. This number, Victory, when these fellas put on the record and called it the second line, we used to play that number I would say about at least a half an hour. But I used to walk the ball all around the tables and everything, and while the band was still playing. And that was one of our most famous numbers down there, you know, what we made plenty of money on.

Let me ask you something, Lionel. When you first had the band there, when you used to play with George Garner, you, Howard and Alec Big Art, and then since we came back there, I don't know, it must have been 10 years later, aren't it, Howard? Years there. Yeah, 10 or 15 years later. We took the same four pieces there. Do you think the music on the records you made sounded much like the music you used to play there? I think so. Do you think there was any difference at all? I mean.
No, I wouldn't say that. I wouldn't say that.
But I'll tell you, when I got there I got a melody of feeling back in me. It looked like I was kind of like a, you know, back in the place.
In my opinion that's the way it really sounded like then.
It's good, except that George was playing banjo.

Well I mean that's the one different, but it gave a little different effect. But normally you can feel a person playing, even though he played banjo or played guitar, it was the same thing happening but I want to say the instrument had a different pitch.
So who's the leader really of that mighty 40? Did you have a leader? I mean it was a big art job. Well me and Lionel Lye used to lead the band.
We'd call the numbers. But not the business.
We'd call the numbers, we'd pick up the numbers, all big artists would go collect the money from the man at night. Paying the band.
How many numbers did you have to play? I mean, did you have many breaks or did you have to play them one after the other?

Sometimes we'd take a good break because we used to cook a big pot. I was at lunch at night back. You know we'd cook, sometimes we'd cook pigtails and rice, stew and rice. We'd have a big pot of food on the fire every night. And we'd take a little break. But some nights we couldn't take too much break because the place was too crowded. We'd have to play with them.
We'd have to play with them. I think that covers most of that kind of business. What happened when you finally left from there? I mean you personally. What would you play with them?
Well that's when I went to the Happy Land and then. You went to the Happy Land and then. Again, I went back to the Happy Land.
Yeah, and I went there with y'all. And then when Pinky got the job at the Melody Inn for this other fellow, I left y'all at the Happy Land and I got another band and went back in the Melody Inn.
Well who did you work with at the Happy Land?

Well first I worked with Idru Coleman, and Albert Giles, and what's that called bass band? Dorsley. Eddie Dorsley. And then after a while, that's when I told you, I left and went back with you again. That's right. And when I went back with him again, after I went with him a while, I know something happened, I think the job ran out over there.

When you came back to the Melody Inn when I had the band in charge, this man would close up and went back to the Happy Land. Yeah, that's right. And then when he came back to the Happy Land, the Melody Inn opened again, I went back to the Melody Inn. And that's where I put Andrew Morgan in my place at the Happy Land.
That's right. And I worked with Andrew Morgan. Was the same outfit with the exception of Idru Coleman?

Yeah, I have a picture of your book in there with Andrew Morgan. Did you have it? Yeah, I have a picture of it. I'd sure like to see it. Yeah, I'll get you a copy of that one. I'll get back. Listen, did you ever make any recordings other than the one with Harold?
Not that I know of, but I already recorded with Cheetah on it, but I never did hear it.

Yeah, that woman in love, who was on that recording that was playing at a store one day, just about three days after that fellow there that night, we made him cut the tape record off, but he had already got the woman in love. Remember Schmidty sang and I played the sweet solo on it.

And then I mean, I'm talking about that Happy Land in 2 there. So I was coming there with the, you used to come out there quite often there. And we had, but this was a new bunch. I had never seen all the equipment for Eddie, but I didn't have an idea it was a tape recorder. It looked like it was mostly taking pictures. But Eddie Dawson said he saw the red light going on, but it must have been a very compact deal. Yeah. So dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear Well you were down there? Well yeah I was in that band. Well when I was in the band one time, I had Ricard was in the band, I was playing first trombone, Ricard playing second, Morris Strange playing trombone. And I had Handy, Edward Bartlett playing alto, he died. And George Clark playing tenor. He was playing alto then.
He had left the clarinet alone at that time.
He had two altos in that band. Two altos. And then they had old man Kimball playing bass. Kimball's daddy. Yeah, Kimball's daddy. And Roy playing drummer, he was a good drummer.
Roy was a good drummer. That's the drummer he used to play with Sam Marvins.
That's right.
After Schein left then they got Roy.
That'd be Roy after that.
Schein, Nolan Williams.

And Benny Turner was playing piano. Yeah, from my Algears. Yeah. No, not that Benny Turner. That Benny Turner used to be an alto player. No. No, Benny Turner's piano player. Well I thought Benny Turner, I didn't know he lived in Algears. I always knew he lived in Goodtown. He lived in Goodtown one hour. He lived in Goodtown one hour. So he lived in Goodtown one hour. So he had their own impression. But you ain't talking about what you call him, living in Goodtown. Not Benny Turner. They always had living across the river. Living across the river. They all had their own presence.
But you ain't talking about what you call living in Goodtown?

Not Benny Toyner. No, he must be talking about. What you call living in Goodtown? Oh man, Benny lived in Goodtown. He wasn't Toyner, he wasn't Benny Toyner. Benny Toyner was the one who used to work with the Sonny South.
That's right.
They're nice.

I know what you're talking about, what you call living on Broadway Street out there. I think he died too. No, he didn't. He worked at the Army Bay State, he played a couple of times, playing time with Pete Bocci, he used it, what is that? What is that? Charlie Hampton. Charlie Hampton. No, not Charlie Hampton.
I'm talking about Benny.
He was a big tall doctor. Big tall Benny. Benny Toyner. He used to work with when he was working at the tenors.
That's right. When he worked at the tenors.
That was John Haynes' band, huh? At the tenors?
Let's see, who had that band that worked at the tenors? No, it was the Louis Daniels. No, wait, what year you was playing at? Oh, I don't know yet. I'll be frank, that's one thing I don't know yet.
Because Kuyper was there for a while. When I was at the tenors? No, no, no. You came after the kind of thing.

When I was in there it was a guitar player, a band-a-gill player's job. For that one? For that one. He taught René Hall and all them for that. He was a very good band-a-gill player and guitar player. What was his name? Willie what? Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Yeah. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor.
Client and piano and the greatest, one of the greatest alto players that ever put an alto

to his mouth. No, no, no. I don't want you. You never met him? Just unassumable as can be, but the finest play you ever play? He never smiled. He's a phenomenal. I'm a smart guy. He's a nice fellow. And even one of the fun times we would have, in fact I would have so many different times I wouldn't know exactly when we'd stop working on that because it'd be one place and there'd be another. We'd work at the, what was it, the Papaw? Oh, Decatur Street. Yeah. Papaw and Decatur Street. We worked at the Lake, remember? That's right. Right near the happening, I don't know what the name was, the place. Mamalu. No, now you're talking about Mamalu. It must be, it suits you. No, you remember when you were- Moro. Yeah, that's right. Moro. Uh-huh. Because every time we look, I was going with Harold someplace.

One thing I was going to ask you, it depends. You know, that band you were talking about with Son Johnson, that was at the Entertainers Club. That was after the band you had with Johnny Handy. Yeah. That's right.

That was after. I can tell that for a reason, because I was away with Walter Pichon, I think. And the band was real good. In fact the band was so good it was a shame that they were making the money. But we were playing in the singing theaters. And I got tired of making those trips and getting through, like we were running through Arkansas and so forth. And we'd go through all the mountains and everything, and we didn't even have a chance to even get a chance to eat and I didn't even have to hit the stage and play those big programs. So I just got disgusted. And when it came past through Memphis I left the band. And as soon as I came in, I was in Ireland and I went with the Entertainers. Tell me something.

Being as good a musician as you are, I'm talking to you, did you ever teach anybody around here to play? I mean did you teach anybody around here? Oh yeah, I teach quite a bit of sports. Anybody in particular? I wouldn't know.

Well I'll tell you, one of those folks I taught, he's very fine saxophone player. In fact I didn't teach him completely but I had him for quite a while. He's still a saxophone player there. He plays with, how do you call this band, Dukes, Raul Dukes? Yeah, Emanuel's son-in-law. What's his name again? Blue, Blue, Blue, Blue, Blue, Blue, Blue. Yeah, uh-huh.
But you taught him to play music on his saxophone. Well I mean I had a,
This is the second reel of Lionel Fairbos. I didn't get your full name.
Lionel Charles Fairbos. Fairbos is what they're trying to pronounce.
Fairbos, huh? I say Fairbos. I hear some people say that, huh?
Well, there's so many different pronunciations. Like, we say, Foybos or Fairbos. Like my son, he pronounces it like the old people. Fairbos.
I see. And you're a senior, though. That's right. He's named after. I wanted to ask you about that ladies band, All Women, huh, in the band?

Oh, yeah. I don't know what outfit it was, but it was a female outfit. We used to play on all from stage. I don't remember which one it was at that time. But it was very fine. So I decided that's what I wanted to play. Were they from where or were they from here?
Well, they were from away. I see. That's why I'm-

Well now, could he get off? Could he get away from the melody much?

Oh yeah, he could, he could improvise, yeah. Oh yeah, he could improvise. And he was a good street man too. Oh yeah. Oh yeah. He could play above all those instruments. You could hear him coming down the street above all those instruments.
Would he play in a ratty, tonk style if he wanted to? He could do that, huh? Yeah, he could improvise, yeah. And he could play the regular street music, the legit style too.
Yeah, because then he went to Chicago, he worked in the theater office for a long time. But he could play, because he used to play dances, I mean, and he'd play all that stuff.
Every brass band is on, you know, the Ormond band. I was just second line. I didn't come from school. Yank and all them.

I work quite a few brass bands, but really not too much. I never liked the idea of the walking. I've been with kids in there, but you mean like organized brass bands?
Well, organized, or jump up, or what have you?
Well I tell you, I work with, like Harold made quite a few brass bands, and then I work with Pajot in the outfit, with Chic.
And Eureka, so. Yeah. And then I work, well I work with quite a few, because I work with Andrew Morgan.
See when Pajot died, he was the one who played with us. See when Pajot died. I remember that. I was there.
And I work with some parades with Andrew Morgan, and with Andrew Jefferson. And, oh, in fact, I've played quite a few parades.
That's in late years, or early years?
Well I mean, I'd say it's been, oh, the last 15 years I guess.
Yeah, I was trying to remember, because I know I had seen you in the street quite a few times. Yeah, that's right. To get all this straightened out in my head, were you playing before depression?

Yeah. They never had many gigs on the side.

Well yeah, but I don't think I was on the third period then when I played at Popeyes. That was before that.
That was before that. Yeah, that was before that.

And even, well I know that because when we worked at the lake, I was newly married. And it's like when I was 18 I was newly married. That was before depression. Sunday morning, I remember when that happened.
I was working at Crescent Bay, the country, the Gravid, and the country. I went home in 42. Did you go in the army? No. You played all during World War II?

Well yeah, at which they had to play, you know what I mean, because for a while they didn't have anything at all to play. Nobody was at the time, like I said, when I was in the WPA, because that's when we used to play the soldiers. We used to play the soldiers away from the parish prison, and then we used to play USO deals. But that was true at WPA. We played at Cavalier-Johnson, Jackson Barracks, up at Camp Prochet. You remember VE Day when Germany surrendered? No, I don't know. I can't really play. You can't recall. You remember when Japan? I can remember, but I can't remember what happened on the-
Yeah, not as clear.

I just wondered if you remember who you were playing with. No, I can't remember. Do you follow boxing? Do you like boxing much? Do you remember where you were playing when different fights were, you know, like championships and all that?

No, I'll be frank with you. I never was much of a sports fan. I mean I enjoy a good fight or a good baseball game or any, even swimming, racing and so forth, but I would be an average sports fan I never was.
Yeah, a lot of guys can remember who they were playing with when Johnson and Jeffrey thought
something like that.
Yeah. I wanted to ask you again about your own playing. What do you believe that a trumpet should do in a band? What kind of part should he take?

Well in my opinion a trumpet should carry a melody so they know what you're playing. And then if you vary it away from the melody, well I mean and then when you're going out you should have some melody involved so they know what you're playing.
Now that's my opinion.
You always believe in some melody. Yeah that's right, to let them know at least what you're playing.
Well what do you think about the changes in music then? Different styles. You mean yourself?

Well you have to change, because even though you play Dixieland, but unless you were just working Dixieland in one particular spot you play all Dixieland, but you have to play Dixieland and then you have to play rock and roll and then what do they call it, this new beat?
Progressive.

Not so much progressive. Bossanova. Oh yeah, Bossanova and Rumba, Sambos, Congo and all that kind of stuff too. But as far as I mean you have to play rock and roll, what do they call it again? Well they've got the twist for a while.
Not with the beat outfit in it.
No I mean it's beat business. It's not rock and roll, it's got another name for it, no.
Oh, progressive jazz, whatever.

It's sort of right, it's just a new interpretation of that man of rock and roll, because when he said you're not rock, you're going to roll and so forth, I mean but now it's a different beat on it. It's between rock and roll and progressive jazz. Swing, that's what I think is between rock and roll and swing because it has the beat.

It's always off the beat, what they play, I know it. It's always off the beat, you play behind the beat all the time. The singing with them dudes is making anything. That's what I mean, yeah. But it's always behind the beat.
Like all these records they make, always behind the beat.
What about your own style? You can play most any style? Oh no, I wouldn't say most any style, no.

But I mean we sort of imitate some styles. I mean but quite naturally each person has the only individual we are playing. But I mean who I would say is covered behind, I would know because I've listened at, when I used to listen to Bernie Berrigan play and you listen to maybe Harry James or you listen to these fallout formations, all the ones I mentioned to Barry about, well you get a little of each one in your playing and then you find that you, in fact, you know I don't play like you and you don't play like me.
You might hear me say I got that little part of what she did in there. I say oh that line myself, you know, except what he did in there. I say go down the line, even going for the rest of the day.
But I never really tried to imitate anybody really.
I always tried to play.

But if something they make you would like. And you were quite nice, you pick up on what somebody else makes. But I mean they said a copy like some of the other ones, copy completely behind Louis Armstrong. Or maybe just like you said Kidron Day or this day there, or Martin Bergman, or Harry James, some folks they patented completely behind them.

But I never did try to imitate really. But it's a dude that something, make something, I mean that's a certain part of playing a number, a little thing he'd make. And I like that. And I get that in my head, I get on my arm, I play that number, I put that in there, and that's what you mean, kind of like, something. I might hear myself, I hear me make it, and it's too easy to hear why I hear me playing it. And you like that? Well that's it easy, you know, I'm only playing seven numbers that's made. Can you play progressive? No.
Bebop? None of that.
Well what they call bebop, I mean I play bebop because I mean I've had it in music and played, but I mean just to only be a bebop player? No.
Tell me about some of the different jobs you played, you know, like good jobs and bad jobs, exciting places and all this.

Well I played some nice jobs because I've seen, I played, when I was with Walter Pichot, we played at the Jung, played at the Roosevelt, played at the Roseanne Restaurant, played at I think it's, I don't know if it was on the one, we played at the Country Club. Those are all nice jobs. I mean of the high type of, and then I played, oh I played just a beer garden with four pieces, three pieces. And anybody played with hand, if you say bad jobs, if we played with hand, we'd work for weeks and wouldn't make a dime. If that was you'd go bad job. See for yourself. The music was good but the pay was no money involved.
See for yourself.
In fact really there was no money involved for years, because I know when we was working at like the time you talk about doing an impression, we used to get a dollar and a half a night.
Did you get tips?
Some places you wouldn't get tips. We'd get a 50 cent tip. Six brits at night. Well I never worked for that. But the kid in there used to work for 75 cents a night, imagine this.
I mean at that time, a dollar and a half, we'd leave there anyway with two dollars, maybe
three dollars. Which was like six or seven dollars. Yeah, and then you know, it'd be the truth. Or even more so.
Did you make more money off the tips than you did off the salary on jobs ever? No. You never got great tips. No.
My boy's father said that they made fifty hundred dollar tips per annum.

I worked in pre-assisting. And when we split the credit, I worked like that, down half of six percent. But we worked, the kid in there, wind up, said if I was getting down half, we wind up making like four dollars a month. Well maybe something like that, but I was talking about it. The kid was rated. Normally, I mean like if you made a Saturday, if you made fifteen or twenty dollars a night,
and the tip would run over that, no uh-uh. No, no, no, no, no.
Were you at Haydell's, that must have been after World War II, huh? Because I was down here. Oh definitely. Yeah, I was down here.

It was around, it couldn't have been.

Well not on the way to Atlanta. But I mean after Atlanta, would you pass going to Washington?
No, you wouldn't pass right now.

Oh, well, well, because I was out where he was, but I was, when you say he was around the coast of Macon, I was in Macon, Georgia, the ice station down there. But I was down here. Robin Field, I was supposed to Savannah, Savannah, Georgia, all that stuff.
I was down here. Because I went to Washington, my son was at that edgewood, right outside of Baltimore,
and we went through Atlanta. Augusta, I was out there, I stood in Augusta about 18 months.

trombone with him. He told me that my brother died about a month or two months ago. Yeah. So what about Bigfoot Bill? Oh yeah, I worked with Bigfoot Bill from time to time too. Yeah, Bigfoot Bill had a little outfit we used to work with. You were with him steady? Well I mean, at the time it would be steady. I mean, maybe two or three months and then I'd move off to somebody else and then I'd move
off to somebody else and then I'd go back with him again because that's good. Job run out with him. Yeah, yeah.
In fact he never did work regular jobs. Did he get a big band or something?

He did a big band or something? Yeah. He did a big band or something? Yeah. He did a big band or something? Yeah. He did a big band or something? Yeah. Yeah. One time he had a big band but most of the time we had about five pieces I think we used to work.

Piccolo, yeah. And Albert Warner himself. Was that kind of a Dixieland band?

Wesson Union place.
I must have met him or whatever. He didn't see him.

What was it like working on the Madisonville? How did that gig work?

Oh it was, you played, when the boat was going over, you played several sets. He played mostly to, I guess, to break the monotonous of the trip because that was the only way you could get across the lake at that time. And they played mostly to break the monotonous of the trip I guess because it was the only way you could get across the lake. He used to hold automobiles and picnic parties and so forth. He would leave from West End and go to Mandeville and Madisonville. But it wasn't a spectacular job, it was just a music job is all I can see. If we came back.

You know something I want to ask you which I remember from Lutchen's, but I wonder about these other places because I can't remember. It's not like playing a regular dance. You see a regular dance, well you're only, it was for participating in the dancing, but here it was a question of getting refreshments and maybe eating a sandwich or something.

He was a nice fellow, too. Prince, man, real fun.

And Walter Pichardt and Kildee, or Clyde Cardone, that's it. Manu Kruzman. That's for John and Brunas. Now do man, he used to do arranging to do the right. Well he used to do it. Yeah, well he used to do all that Dix-Land stuff. In fact I have Dix-Land stuff. I got some music. I have Dix-Land stuff. I got some music. I got it. I said I'm going to keep that long.
Arrange with these this room. Oh yeah, all those old numbers, all the Scott Jopper music and all the music.

segments.title: Opening: date, location and birth date
segments.summary: Interviewers confirm the date, 3 August 1964, the place (Ferbos's house) and his birth date of July 17, 1911.

segments.title: Why he took up music; teacher Shawnee
segments.summary: No one in his family played; seeing a women's band at a theater made him want to play. Harold Dejan adds that the teacher charged 25 cents a lesson.

segments.title: Cornet to trumpet and later teachers
segments.summary: He began on cornet, moved to trumpet, took lessons about two years with Shawnee then Manuel Perez and others, learning theory and reading.

segments.title: First bands: Starlight Serenade and house parties
segments.summary: He recalls his first band, its members, the two trumpets, playing house parties for small pay, and moving on to better outfits.

segments.title: The Moonlight Serenaders and their personnel
segments.summary: Ferbos and Dejan reconstruct who played in the next band, mostly stock orchestrations.

segments.title: Playing head arrangements versus writing out parts
segments.summary: Dejan explains that Ferbos, a first-trumpet man, wrote out any requested number and put it in front of him instead of playing by head.

segments.title: Admired trumpeters: Cuckoo, Dumaine, Duran, Perez, Kid Rena
segments.summary: Ferbos recalls hearing Louis Dumaine, Maurice Durand, Manuel Perez and Kid Rena; Dejan tells of Rena's stamina at the Gypsy Tea Room.

segments.title: Buddy Petit, Ferbos's own trumpet style, and Gaudet
segments.summary: Asked whether he sounded like the older trumpeters, Ferbos says his style has changed; Dejan places him with the musically able Perez-type players, and they mention Gaudet.

segments.chapter: The Melody Inn and the Mighty Four
segments.title: How the Melody Inn job came about
segments.summary: Dejan tells how a drummer heard from a music store of a band job at the Melody Inn for Mr. Highdown; the band started on the floor of a lunch place.

segments.chapter: The Melody Inn and the Mighty Four
segments.title: Working the Melody Inn: hours, nights and repertoire
segments.summary: Nine-to-two sets, Friday through Sunday, a request program of pop tunes, Dixieland, rumbas and tangos, with Ferbos writing choruses.

segments.chapter: The Melody Inn and the Mighty Four
segments.title: Crowds at the Melody Inn and why it closed
segments.summary: Musicians and packed crowds came; the owner had a heart attack, sold the place and died, and the band moved to Happy Land.

segments.chapter: The Melody Inn and the Mighty Four
segments.title: Pianists and naming the band the Mighty Four
segments.summary: Frank Moyer, Wiggins and then Smitty held the piano chair; the group became the Mighty Four, and a second-line number made good money.

segments.chapter: The Melody Inn and the Mighty Four
segments.title: Sound of the Mighty Four, leadership and breaks
segments.summary: Ferbos and Dejan compare the later recording with the old sound, say they called numbers while the bassist collected pay, and describe cooking during breaks.

segments.chapter: Happy Land, sidemen and other bands
segments.title: Moves between the Happy Land and the Melody Inn
segments.summary: Ferbos went to Happy Land with Idru Coleman and others, returned to Dejan, and Andrew Morgan replaced Dejan at Happy Land.

segments.chapter: Happy Land, sidemen and other bands
segments.title: A recording at Happy Land and an earlier big-band lineup
segments.summary: Dejan recalls a song recorded unnoticed at Happy Land; the talk turns to a band's members with two altos and a Kimball on bass.

segments.chapter: Happy Land, sidemen and other bands
segments.title: Sorting out the sidemen: Roy, Nolan Williams, the two Bennys
segments.summary: The three argue over which Benny Turner or Benny Toyner played piano and where he lived, and recall a drummer named Roy.

segments.chapter: Happy Land, sidemen and other bands
segments.title: Who led the band at the Tenors; guitarist Willie O'Connor
segments.summary: They try to recall bandleaders at the Tenors and a fine banjo and guitar player who taught others.

segments.chapter: Happy Land, sidemen and other bands
segments.title: Places worked, the Entertainers Club and leaving Pichon's tour
segments.summary: Ferbos lists spots he and Dejan worked and says he quit Walter Pichon's theater tour at Memphis after hard travel, then joined the Entertainers.

segments.chapter: Happy Land, sidemen and other bands
segments.title: Ferbos as a teacher
segments.summary: He says he has taught quite a few students, including a saxophonist now in a local band.

segments.chapter: Reel 2: Perez, brass bands and early life
segments.title: Pronunciation of the name Ferbos
segments.summary: Start of reel 2; Ferbos gives his full name and discusses how the family name is pronounced.

segments.chapter: Reel 2: Perez, brass bands and early life
segments.title: The women's band that inspired him
segments.summary: He describes an all-women outfit on a touring circuit whose trumpet players made him want to play trumpet.

segments.chapter: Reel 2: Perez, brass bands and early life
segments.title: Manuel Perez, the wah-wah mute and Chicago
segments.summary: Ferbos says Perez may have been first with the wah-wah mute, could improvise, and carried above the street band; he later worked in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Reel 2: Perez, brass bands and early life
segments.title: Playing brass bands and parades
segments.summary: He played some brass bands and parades with Pajeaud, Andrew Morgan and Andrew Jefferson, mostly in the last fifteen years.

segments.title: Depression years, the WPA band, his 1934 marriage and the return of beer
segments.summary: Ferbos played in the WPA band through the Depression, married in 1934 while with Pichon, and played with Handy when beer returned.

segments.title: Pearl Harbor and war-time playing at army posts
segments.summary: He recalls the WPA band at Jackson Barracks on Pearl Harbor Sunday and playing for soldiers and USO shows; he is not a sports fan.

segments.title: What a trumpet should do in a band
segments.summary: Ferbos believes a trumpeter should carry the melody so listeners know what is being played.

segments.title: Changing styles: rock and roll, bossa nova and beat
segments.summary: They discuss having to play Dixieland, rock, bossa nova and the new beat, and agree the records are played behind the beat.

segments.title: His own style, influences and bebop
segments.summary: Ferbos says he picks up bits from others rather than imitating, and will play bebop but is not a bebop player.

segments.title: Good jobs, bad jobs and early pay and tips
segments.summary: He lists high-class jobs with Pichon and beer-garden gigs that paid almost nothing, such as a dollar and a half a night.

segments.title: Where Dick Allen first heard him; Allen's Georgia roots and army years
segments.summary: Allen says he heard the band at Haydell's about 1950-51; talk drifts to Allen's Georgia hometown and where Ferbos and Dejan were stationed.

segments.title: Playing with Fats Domino and Harrison
segments.summary: Dejan says Fats Domino played with him and speaks of working with Harrison.

segments.title: Why Wednesday nights were poor
segments.summary: Ferbos says the added Wednesday night lasted a few weeks because working people stay home early in the week.

segments.title: Herbert Smith and the Last Roundup
segments.summary: They recall saxophonist Herbert Smith, his restaurant and bartending job, and the Last Roundup place.

segments.title: Who played at Haydell's
segments.summary: Ferbos lists Dejan, Gano, himself and a rotation of pianists ending with John Smith; the four stayed together two or three years.

segments.title: Walter Pichon's band
segments.summary: Ferbos names Pichon's members, including Raymond Brown on trumpet, Judge Riley on drums and saxophonists, and then Nat Story.

segments.title: Nat Story, the King brothers and Robichaud's band
segments.summary: They recall Nat Story, trombone-playing brothers, Albert Snyder and Joe Robichaud's band.

segments.title: Working with Bigfoot Bill
segments.summary: Ferbos worked on and off with Bigfoot Bill's small band, including Maurice Justin and Hippolyte Francis.

segments.title: Joe Benoit's Dixieland band
segments.summary: He recalls playing with Joe Benoit, Albert Warner and his son Piccolo; Benoit died recently.

segments.title: Madisonville boat band: personnel
segments.summary: Ferbos names the players on the lake boat to Madisonville, including two men named Reuben, and Dejan adds remarks about Davis.

segments.title: How the Madisonville boat job worked
segments.summary: The band played sets on the hour-long trip across the lake from West End; they cannot recall whether they stayed overnight.

segments.title: Lutchen's and playing two numbers then resting
segments.summary: Ferbos explains that bands played a few numbers then paused so patrons would drink; they talk about Lutchen's.

segments.title: Playing with Sweet Emma and Celestin
segments.summary: Ferbos played with Emma off and on, took calls by phone from anybody, and played with Celestin when Kildee and Ormond Franklin were in the band.

segments.title: Writing arrangements; Kildee and Herman Franklin
segments.summary: Ferbos wrote arrangements for Moonlight Serenaders; they praise Kildee as an arranger and discuss Herman Franklin's career with Celestin.

segments.title: Other local arrangers and Ferbos's music collection
segments.summary: Ferbos names other New Orleans arrangers and says he keeps his old Dixieland stock arrangements and Scott Joplin music.
